title: PATIENT ASSESSMENT, REASSESSMENT AND VITAL SIGNS
knowledge: State the nurse's role and responsibility in completing a Comprehensive Patient Assessment, Reassessment and Vital Signs for a patient in area of practice and comparing findings with the patient's baseline findings are so important to overall assessment.
Verbalize the role and responsibilities of the nurse and the need to start the assessment with taking a full Health History, family history, psychosocial history and activities of daily living.
Discuss why assessment involves collecting both subjective and objective data of the presenting complaint.
Explain why observing the patient's body language during assessment is important.

State the PQRSTP model of exploring the chief complaint i.e. Proactive or palliative (provokes or relieves symptoms), quality or quantity (what does symptom/s feel, look or sound like), region or radiation (where is the symptom/s) severity of symptom/s including PAIN SCORE, timing (when was it sudden, how often and how long does symptom/s last), psychosocial history, (find out how the patient feels about himself, his place in society and his relationships with others).

Explain how to properly observe the patient using 'some teams' – symmetry (are face and body symmetrical!?), old (do they look their age?), mentation (are they alert confused agitated or inattentive?), expression (do they appear ill, in pain or anxious?) trunk (are they thin, stocky, obese or barrel-chested?), extremities (are the fingers clubbed, are there joint abnormalities or edema?), appearance (are they clean and appropriately dressed?), movement (is their posture, gait and coordination normal, are they mobile and able to ambulate normally?), speech (is their speech relaxed, clear, strong, understandable and appropriate, do they sound stressed?).
Verbalize the standard for the frequency of measuring vital signs as per policy in area of practice.
Discuss the weight and height, temperature and pain score as vital signs and why these are important.
State how to assess the pulse noting rate, rhythm and strength and why these are important when considering the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat.
Discuss the rationale for not using the thumb for taking a pulse or blood pressure.
Discuss the limitations of measuring oxygen saturation with pulse oximeter.
State when manual blood pressure readings and pulses are preferable to automated readings.
Explain and calculate the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) i.e. SBP +2 x DBP/3 and why this is important note.
Explore the observations and parameters for reporting significant findings and vital signs to nurse in charge and/or physician.
Discuss the need and how to document the patient's comprehensive assessment, reassessment and vital signs findings and at the time of completion.
skills: Demonstrate how to complete a comprehensive patient assessment, reassessment and vital signs of a patient in area of practice and compare findings with the patient's baseline results and explain why this comparison data is so important to the overall assessment of the patient and the chief complaint.
Complete an assessment on a patient with taking a full health history e.g. biographic data, chief complaint, medical history, family history, psychosocial history and activities of daily living.
Demonstrate the collecting of both subjective and objective data when completing an assessment.
List and demonstrate some examples of the patient's body language noted during the completion of an assessment and state what message/s the patient might have been communicating.

Demonstrate the use of the PQRST model of exploring the chief complaint i.e. proactive or palliative (provokes or relieves symptoms), quality or quantity (what does symptoms/s feel, look or sound like), region or radiation (where is the symptom/s) severity of symptom/s including PAIN SCORE, timing (when, was it sudden, how often and how does symptom/s last).

Complete an observation of a patient using 'some teams' – symmetry (are face and body symmetrical?), old (do they look their age?) mentation (are they alert, confused agitated or inattentive?), expression (do they appear ill, in pain or anxious?), trunk (are they thin, stocky, obese or barrel-chested?), extremities (are the fingers clubbed, are there joint abnormalities or edema?) appearance (are they clean and appropriately dressed?), movement (is their posture, gait and coordination normal, are they mobile and able to ambulate normally?) Speech (is their speech relaxed, clear, strong, understandable and appropriate, do they sound stressed?).
Complete the documentation for the frequency of measuring vital signs as per policy in area of practice.
Demonstrate taking the weight and height, temperature and pain score as vital signs.
Demonstrate how to assess the pulse noting rate, rhythm and strength and why these are important when considering the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat.
Complete the measuring of oxygen saturation with pulse oximeter.
Complete both manual blood pressure readings and pulse and automated readings.
Demonstrate how to read and calculate the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP).
Complete the documentation and reporting of significant findings and vital signs to nurse in charge and/or physician.
Complete the documentation of the patient's comprehensive assessment, reassessment and vital signs accurately.
attitude: Accept constructive criticism as learning opportunity/s.
To be self-aware of limitation in knowledge and skills.
To be approachable and open to answer patient and family's questions.
Deal with and manage patient information professionally with confidentiality and integrity.

Demonstrate ability to organize and facilitate a reflection session in and on practice after a learning opportunity occurs during the completion of a comprehensive assessment, reassessment and vital signs of patient needs and activate findings to improve future practice and response.

title: SBAR ENDORSEMENT AND HANDOVER COMMUNICATION
knowledge: Explain the rationale for a standardized method which facilitates the effective and efficient communication of appropriate patient information between clinical staff involved with the care a patient.
Explore the transitioning of care i.e. when there is a change of responsibility and authority.
Explain what it means to have patients of concern i.e. patients handed over in accordance with their severity and clinical risk, as determined by the treating healthcare practitioner.

Discuss effective communication i.e. reduces errors and improves patient safety, timely, accurate, complete and not vague. The information is understood by recipient (clarifying questions must be asked to achieve this), limit interruptions during communication and use the standardized SBAR tool.

List the barriers to effective communication such as: people do not listen to each other, fatigue, cultural norms, multitasking, stress, physicians and nurses are trained to communicate differently and many nurses are uncomfortable giving patient care recommendations to physicians.

Discuss the components of SBAR Tool:
    S = Situation
    B = Background
    A = Assessment
    R = Recommendations

Explore the benefits of SBAR i.e. improved communication as helps everyone understand the overall picture, critical language is clear and not vague, situational awareness provides for an ongoing dialogue, planning and thinking ahead and patient safety is improved.
Explain how to document using the SBAR tool.
skills: Demonstrates why a standardized method which facilitates the effective and efficient communication of appropriate patient information between clinical staff involved with the care of a patient is necessary in area of practice.
Show the transitioning of care i.e. when there is a change of responsibility and authority.
Demonstrate what it means to have patients of concern i.e. patients handed over in accordance with their severity and clinical risk, as determined by the treating healthcare practitioner.

Demonstrate effective communication i.e. reduces errors and improves patient safety, timely, accurate, complete and not vague. The information is understood by recipient (clarifying questions must be asked to achieve this), limit interruption during communication and use the standardized SBAR tool.

Show how to overcome the barriers to effective communication such as: people do not listen to each other, fatigue, cultural norms, multitasking, stress, physicians and nurses are trained to communicate differently and many nurses are uncomfortable giving patient care recommendations to physician.

Demonstrate the components of the SBAR tool:
    S = Situation
    B = Background
    A = Assessment
    R = Recommendation
Demonstrate how to document using the SBAR tool.
attitude: Accept constrictive criticism as learning opportunity.
To be self-aware of limitation in knowledge and skills.
To be approachable and open to answer patient and family's questions relate to their care or endorsement and handover.
Attentive to overall patient experience e.g. pain. Anxiety and have ability to provide comfort and emotional support as needed.

Demonstrate ability to organize and facilitate a reflection session in and on practice after communication using the SBAR tool provides a learning opportunity and activate findings to improve future practice and response.
